args.request: Turn article.txt about tiny urban forests into a podcast chat between two hosts, friendly curious back-and-forth, one male and one female English voice, roughly 90 seconds, no music, finished audio not just script, no made-up facts.

story.title: Tiny Forests podcast
story.setting: A cosy small podcast studio with two microphones on a wooden desk, warm soft lamp light, realistic look.

subjects.words: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length dark hair and a green sweater, speaking in a warm, curious British English voice
A man in his thirties with short brown hair, a beard and a blue shirt, speaking in a friendly, relaxed English voice

beats.text: Two hosts sit at the desk chatting into microphones, medium shot.
spoken: Maya: So Tom, I read about tiny forests this week. Have you heard of them?
Maya: Ha, no! Cities across Europe and Asia are turning empty lots, about the size of a tennis court, into really dense little forests.

beats.text: The hosts keep chatting, medium shot.
spoken: Tom: Okay, how do you make a forest that small?
Maya: It is a method from Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. You plant three to five native saplings per square metre, in enriched soil.
Tom: Wow, that is packed in tight.

beats.text: The hosts keep chatting, medium shot.
spoken: Maya: That is the point. The trees compete for light, so they grow quickly.
Tom: And then what, you just leave it?
Maya: Supporters say it can become self-sustaining in about three years.

beats.text: The hosts keep chatting, medium shot.
spoken: Tom: So what do cities get out of it?
Maya: Advocates point to cooler streets, more insects and birds, and a place for schoolchildren to learn.
Tom: I love that. But is there a catch?

beats.text: The hosts keep chatting, medium shot.
spoken: Maya: Critics say the evidence is still thin. Lots of projects are too young to measure.
Tom: Right, and with all that crowding, I guess not every sapling makes it?
Maya: Exactly. Dense planting can mean many saplings die.

beats.text: The hosts keep chatting and smile at the end, medium shot.
spoken: Maya: Urban ecologists agree on one thing: a tiny forest is not a substitute for protecting existing large trees.
Tom: Because the big trees store far more carbon. Good to know!
